title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
This is the title page and opening of the introduction of E410 (Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 20, written 1771, printed 1776). It contains no formulas. Euler sets out his programme and its limits.
(1) Everything the geometers have produced so far on the shape of flexible and elastic bodies applies only to simple threads (fila simplicia), whether perfectly flexible or resisting bending through rigidity or elasticity. The threads may be loaded by arbitrary forces.
(2) The known results on the curvature of linen and sails are acceptable only so far as those shapes reduce to the curvature of a simple thread. This alludes to the lintearia and velaria problems of Jakob and Johann Bernoulli.
(3) All known results are further restricted to plane curves.
(4) Therefore we are very far from a complete theory that would determine the shape of flexible surfaces and of flexible solid bodies. That theory is so hidden that not even its first principles have been worked out.
(5) Euler declines to attempt it here. On the next page he says he will instead treat simple threads, both flexible and elastic, from 'true and general principles'. These principles should give both equilibrium and motion, and should replace earlier solutions built on particular or unclear principles.
The General Problem then follows on the next page: for a thread in equilibrium under arbitrary forces, find the state of tension or bending at each element. Euler's method imagines cutting the thread at a point M, so that each part acts on the other with a force and a couple. In modern terms the page motivates the derivation of the balance laws of force and moment for rods.

ideas.what: The statement that existing theory of flexible and elastic bodies covers only one-dimensional threads in a plane. Sails and linen are handled only by reduction to threads.
ideas.modern_name: Limits of 18th-century rod/string theory: planar elastica, catenary, velaria, lintearia
ideas.usually_credited_to: Historical assessment usually drawn from Truesdell (1960), discussing the Bernoullis and Euler
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638-1788 (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: A programmatic call for a complete theory of the equilibrium and motion of flexible and elastic surfaces and three-dimensional bodies. Euler says its first principles are still unknown.
ideas.modern_name: Theory of plates and shells; three-dimensional continuum mechanics (stress tensor)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Plates: Sophie Germain, Lagrange, Poisson, Navier, Kirchhoff. 3D stress: Cauchy (1822-23).
ideas.where_published: Euler's attempt at surfaces in E302 (Tentamen de sono campanarum, 1766). Discussed by Truesdell.

ideas.what: Announcement that the thread problem will be treated from general principles valid for both equilibrium and motion. This is the setting for the cut principle that follows.
ideas.modern_name: Euler's cut principle; balance of linear and angular momentum for rods
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410 and related papers of the 1770s), per Truesdell
ideas.where_published: E410 and following pages; Truesdell's commentary in Opera omnia II 11/2

deep.surprise_reason: This is an introductory, programmatic page. Euler's admission that a theory of flexible surfaces and solids was lacking is well known and is discussed by Truesdell. Nothing here is new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: 'quam a viribus quibuscunque sollicitata accipiunt est inquisitum' — the image shows a comma after 'accipiunt' is absent, but the sense is 'accipiunt, est inquisitum'.
Page number '381' — the scan shows '381' (the last digit is partly blurred but legible).
